title: Charity that keeps flowing
hookLine: a well, a tree, knowledge taught: good that runs after you're gone (Muslim)

lines: A BENCH WITH A BRASS PLATE.
cards: A park bench with a small brass plate: in memory of someone nobody sitting there has met. A tree someone's grandfather planted, still shading people who don't know his name.
A teacher long gone, whose way of explaining fractions is still passed from one kid to the next. Most of what people do is gone by evening. A few things keep running long after they've stopped.
The hadith has a name for those things, and it's a picture of water.

teach.b: Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: when a person dies, their deeds come to an end, except for three. A charity that keeps flowing. Knowledge people keep benefiting from.
And a righteous child who prays for them. The first is sadaqah jariyah.
Jariyah means running, flowing, like a stream: charity that keeps paying out after the giver has gone. One example is a real well.

teach.h: UTHMAN BUYS THE WELL OF RUMAH.
teach.b: The reports say that in Medina a well called Rumah belonged to a man who sold its water, and the Muslims were short of it. The Prophet asked who would buy the well and make it free for everyone.
The companion Uthman bought it, the reports in Tirmidhi say, and gave it away. People say that well still gives water today. Trees are the second picture.
Bukhari and Muslim report that whenever a Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it's charity for them, every bite, for as long as it grows.

teach.h: A SAPLING IN YOUR HAND AT THE END.
teach.b: And in another report the Prophet said: if the Hour comes and one of you has a sapling in his hand, let him plant it. Even at the end of the world, plant.

Over the centuries, Muslims turned this into institutions: endowments called waqf that paid for hospitals, schools, public fountains and travelers' inns, some still running long after their founders died.
But it doesn't need to be big. Teaching a child to read is flowing knowledge. A recipe passed on.
Something you start that keeps going without you.

how: Muslims give sadaqah jariyah by funding wells, planting trees, endowing schools and mosques, and teaching, and often make it on behalf of parents who have died.

o: charity given only in the month of Ramadan
charity paid out in water, wells and rivers
charity that keeps doing good after you're gone

games.q: what's inside sadaqah jariyah — tap the pairs.
p: plant it, even at the Hour

s: the hadith names three things that continue after death
flowing charity, beneficial knowledge, and a righteous child who prays (Muslim).
only big projects like hospitals count as flowing charity
a tree, a well, or a child taught to read all keep giving.
a hadith says to plant a sapling even if the Hour has come
if one of you has a sapling in his hand, let him plant it (Ahmad; al-Adab al-Mufrad).

games.q: Medina's best well belongs to a man who sells its water, and people are thirsty. the Prophet ﷺ asks who will buy it. you're Uthman. what do you do?
o: buy it and sell the water at a fair price
buy it and make it free for everyone
dig a private well of your own
games.why: Uthman bought the well of Rumah and gave it away (Tirmidhi). people say it still gives water today.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you do well, cooking a dish, fixing a bike, reciting a short surah, writing a letter, calming a crying baby, and one person who'd be helped by learning it.
Or picture a seed going into soil, in a pot, a yard or a community garden, and the shade it might give when you're not there. If you pray, you can intend one of them as sadaqah jariyah.

wordCard.voice: Sadaqah jariyah. Flowing charity: a well, a tree, knowledge taught, good that keeps running after you're gone. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the well keeps giving. Some good keeps running without you. Day one hundred fifty-three.
